rows: In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student deserves to know what they are expected to learn, why it matters, and what quality work looks like. Students need time to practice essential grade-level knowledge and skills and see how their learning connects to their lives.
Two 100% commitments: purpose explained; examples analyzed with scales.
Support to Take the Next Step

Families can count on consistent learning expectations across schools, and students have the time they need to meet them.

Kentucky Priority Standards: Learning and Purpose

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student-standard opportunities** meeting the expectation below. At the start of instruction on each Priority Standard, teachers establish the learning and its purpose. Students explain **WHAT they are learning, WHY it matters and where they can use it**, in their own words, and connect their work to that purpose.
Students can see a purpose for today's work and understand where they might use what they are learning.
100% commitment. Record WHAT and WHY separately; count as met only when both are evident.

They identify **specific features that meet the criteria** and explain what to apply in their own work.
Studying examples makes what quality work looks like visible before students are expected to produce it themselves.
100% commitment · Measure 1. Reporting home: Learning with Purpose → Proficiency Scales.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students deepen their understanding when they do the thinking, connect ideas across subjects, and apply what they know to real problems. We work with families, community members, and local employers to design challenges that matter to students and to Fleming County. Through these experiences, students build the knowledge, skills, and confidence to contribute to their community and compete globally.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students should have a real say in what they explore, how they approach their work, and how they show what they know. When students bring their interests, strengths, talents, cultural knowledge, and lived experiences to their work, they help shape what happens in the classroom and take greater ownership of their learning.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student deserves meaningful opportunities to show what they know and can do through writing, performances, projects, portfolios, and presentations. Above all, their work should provide clear evidence of grade-level and real-world readiness by showing how well they apply the knowledge and skills expected at their grade level to solve problems, make decisions, and communicate their thinking in authentic situations. Their work should also reflect who they are, what interests them, and what they aspire to do.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students should receive feedback tied to clear expectations for mastery while they still have time to act on it. Students use Proficiency Scales to study examples, recognize what quality work looks like, and check their own work in progress. With timely feedback, they can see where they stand, decide what to improve, and take ownership of their next step.
Support to Take the Next Step

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student deserves access to challenging grade-level learning and just-in-time support when they need it. Effective support helps students work through difficulty, do the thinking themselves, and take their next step with greater independence.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student can grow from where they are, master important knowledge and skills, build readiness for the next grade and life beyond school, and develop the agency to shape their own learning and future. Thriving also means feeling a sense of belonging, knowing yourself, developing socially and emotionally, and building habits that support physical health.

Students apply **grade-level knowledge and skills to an authentic problem, need or decision** connected to life, community or work. They explain who is affected, compare possible responses and **justify a solution or recommendation with evidence**.
Students learn to weigh evidence and make decisions they can explain when they face a real problem.

They explain their reasons, how their choices shaped the work and **how the work meets shared learning expectations**.
Meaningful choices help students take responsibility for their work and think through the decisions they make.

Interests, Passions, Aspirations, Skills and Talents

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student learning experiences** meeting the expectation below. Students connect a specific task, product or investigation to **their interests, passions, strengths, skills, talents, cultural knowledge, lived experiences or aspirations**. They explain how that connection shaped their work and identify **a further learning or career possibility** to explore.
Students see how who they are and what they care about can shape what they learn and what they might pursue.

Students **write weekly in every course** to explain reasoning, interpret evidence or communicate subject knowledge. Teachers give feedback on **thinking and relevant writing criteria**; dated samples show student-generated ideas.
Writing makes students' thinking visible and gives them practice communicating clearly in every subject.

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **individual performance-assessment records** meeting the expectation below. Students **apply standards through products, performances or explanations**. Teachers share criteria in advance, assess **each student's demonstrated learning** and give feedback. Evidence from more than one piece of work gives students, families, and teachers a clearer picture of what students can do with their learning.

Teachers provide preparation, accessible participation and feedback that students use to refine goals. Students select relevant BPI portfolio artifacts and explain what each demonstrates; record the district's presentation schedule.
Students learn to explain their progress using evidence they selected and can discuss with others.

Students **contribute ideas, explain reasoning, listen and build on or question peer thinking** toward a shared learning purpose. Each student explains their contribution, what they learned and **how a peer's thinking improved their understanding or work**. Teachers ensure equitable participation.

Students can carry forward what worked and make a practical plan for a challenge they are likely to face again.

Growth Across All Grades and Content Areas

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student learning-goal records in each grade and content area** with evidence of learning growth toward the documented goal. Growth is evaluated in **all grade levels and all subjects and content areas**, including and extending beyond reading and mathematics. Students and teachers compare **earlier and later evidence against the same learning expectation and criteria**. Students explain what improved and what helped. Teachers monitor **individual learning goals**, including for students already above expectations, and respond when progress is insufficient. Report separately the proportion with comparable evidence and the proportion demonstrating growth toward the documented goal; missing evidence does not establish no growth.
Students and families can see how far learning has moved from the student's starting point and what deserves attention next.
Show the work or record that demonstrates growth across all grades and content areas. What changed, and what is the next step?

Comparable dated work, aligned individual assessments, next-step tasks, student goals/decisions and accessible well-being feedback. For growth, mastery, readiness and agency, include all grades and content areas and report coverage and findings by grade/content area.
Mastery Across All Grades and Content Areas

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student-standard records in each grade and content area** meeting the expectation below. Mastery is **expected and evaluated in all grade levels and all content areas**. Students demonstrate **the standard's expected knowledge, skills and thinking** through aligned individual evidence and required accommodations. Teachers use shared criteria and sufficient evidence for the claim; **3.0 represents expected learning where scales apply**. Effort, completion and group performance are reported separately from mastery.
Students and families can see which essential learning students have demonstrated and where more practice or support is needed.
Show the work or record that demonstrates mastery across all grades and content areas. What changed, and what is the next step?

Comparable dated work, aligned individual assessments, next-step tasks, student goals/decisions and accessible well-being feedback. For growth, mastery, readiness and agency, include all grades and content areas and report coverage and findings by grade/content area.

Readiness is **expected and evaluated in all grade levels and all content areas**. Teachers identify **the demands of the next grade, course, pathway or opportunity**. Students demonstrate the relevant knowledge, skills and independence in aligned tasks, explain their evidence and identify gaps. Teachers provide **targeted preparation and opportunities to apply learning in a new context**.
Students and families can see how today's learning prepares students for the demands of their next step.
Show the work or record that demonstrates readiness across all grades and content areas. What changed, and what is the next step?

Comparable dated work, aligned individual assessments, next-step tasks, student goals/decisions and accessible well-being feedback. For growth, mastery, readiness and agency, include all grades and content areas and report coverage and findings by grade/content area.

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student well-being responses** meeting the expectation below. Students experience **safety, belonging and supportive relationships**, identify a trusted adult and know how to obtain help. Leaders use student feedback, attendance and participation to identify barriers and unmet social, emotional or physical needs, **respond promptly and check whether support helped**.
Feeling connected and knowing where to turn for support help students participate in school and stay engaged in learning.

Proficiency Scales: Check Work in Progress

Students learn to spot what their own work needs while they can still improve it.

Across experiences, students explain **how their decisions affected learning** and take increasing responsibility for next steps.
Students build the independence to make thoughtful decisions and adjust their approach when a plan needs to change.

Teachers provide **aligned Proficiency Scales for Priority Standards**. Students use them throughout learning to analyze and discuss examples before their first demonstration, check work in progress at least once during instruction, identify next steps and improve their work. Example analysis and self-checks are reported as **two separate accountability measures**.

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **learning-design records** meeting the expectation below. Teachers develop learning experiences **in partnership with families, community members and local workforce partners**. Partners help frame problems, contribute expertise or define authentic success criteria. Plans and student explanations show **how partner input shaped the learning**, with opportunities accessible to all students. Record each contributor group and its design contribution; audience attendance alone does not establish co-design. A single partnership finding does not establish all elements of a qualifying vibrant learning experience.
Partners help students understand who faces the problem, what is at stake, and what a workable response would look like.
Show the work or record that demonstrates community partnerships in learning design. What changed, and what is the next step?

Task designs, identified standards, student reasoning and products. For partner design, record the contributor, group, input, design change and date; assess student learning separately from partner participation.

Accountability measure: percentage of reviewed **student feedback opportunities** meeting the expectation below. Teachers and peers provide **specific feedback tied to the standard or scale while there is time to use it**. Feedback identifies a feature of the work, what meets the expectation and what needs improvement. Students explain **what they will do next**.
Timely, specific feedback helps students know where to focus their effort before the work is finished.
Show the work or record that demonstrates timely feedback aligned to mastery. What changed, and what is the next step?

Aligned scales, annotated examples, work-in-progress checks, feedback, before/after work, reassessment and common-scoring records. Keep exemplar analysis and self-check results in their separate reporting homes.
